content: Substance-specific mass media campaigns targeting young individuals are commonly implemented as a strategy to prevent illicit drug use. These campaigns are designed to decrease drug use and enhance awareness of the associated risks and problems. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of mass media campaigns in either preventing or reducing illicit drug use, or the intention to use such substances, among young people. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, EMBASE, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses A&I. The search covered studies published from as early as 1861 up to February 2013. The inclusion criteria for the review encompassed cluster-randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective and retrospective cohort studies, interrupted time series (ITS), and controlled before-and-after (CBA) studies. These studies needed to assess the impact of mass media campaigns on drug use, the intention to use drugs, or attitudes toward illicit drugs among individuals under the age of 26. A total of 23 studies, involving 188,934 young participants, were included in the analysis. These studies were conducted in the United States, Canada, and Australia between 1991 and 2012. Among these, 12 were RCTs, two were prospective cohort studies, one was a combination of an RCT and a prospective cohort study, six were ITS studies, and two were CBA studies. The RCTs generally exhibited a low risk of bias, as did the ITS studies, except for the dimension assessing formal test of trend. The prospective cohort studies were of good quality overall, though they lacked detailed descriptions of loss to follow-up based on exposure. Illicit drug use was assessed using a variety of self-reported measures and biomarker-based assessments. These measures were derived from both published and unpublished scales, which made direct comparisons across studies challenging. When data from five RCTs (involving 5,470 participants) were pooled, the results indicated no significant effect of media campaign interventions on drug use (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.02; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.15 to 0.12). Additionally, data from five ITS studies (involving 26,405 participants) specifically examined methamphetamine use. Among four pooled estimates (representing two endpoints measured in two different age groups), a reduction in past-year methamphetamine use was observed only in the 12to 17-year-old age group. However, this effect was not consistent across all measures. Five additional studies, which could not be included in the meta-analyses, reported varied outcomes related to drug use. These studies included one RCT combined with a prospective cohort study, two prospective cohort studies, two ITS studies, and one CBA study, involving a total of 151,508 participants. The results from these studies were mixed, with one study reporting a clear iatrogenic effect (where the campaign inadvertently increased drug use) and another reporting a reduction in drug use. In conclusion, the current body of evidence does not provide sufficient clarity to determine the overall effectiveness of mass media campaigns in reducing illicit drug use among young people. The findings highlight the need for further high-quality research to better understand the impact of these interventions.
